metadata.subtitle: 22 Sections · 8 Thematic Phases · 1400–2800+ Rating Invariants, Templates & Recognition

phases.name: Phase 1: Linear Sweeps & Core Range Structures
phases.description: Greedy exchange foundations, static/2D/geometric line sweeps, difference arrays, Fenwick trees (BIT), Segment Trees (lazy, beats, persistent), and Merge Sort Trees.

phases.name: Phase 2: Tree Algorithms & Structural Hierarchies
phases.description: Binary lifting, LCA, Euler tours, Tree DP, Tree rerooting DP, Heavy-Light Decomposition (HLD), Centroid Decomposition, and Sack (DSU on Tree).

phases.name: Phase 3: Advanced Data Structures & Sqrt Techniques
phases.description: Sqrt decomposition, Mo's algorithm on arrays & trees, Sparse Tables, Cartesian Trees, Persistent Segment Trees, Treaps, PBDS, and Link-Cut Trees.

phases.name: Phase 4: Graph Algorithms & Network Flow
phases.description: Dijkstra variants, 0-1 BFS, Floyd-Warshall, Topo-DP, Kosaraju/Tarjan SCC, 2-SAT, MST variants, Dinic max flow, Min-Cut modeling, and MCMF.

phases.name: Phase 5: Dynamic Programming & Advanced Greedy
phases.description: Monotone queue/stack DP, Convex Hull Trick (CHT), Li Chao Tree, D&C DP, Knuth Optimization, SOS DP, Slope Trick, WQS/Aliens trick, and Matroid theory.

phases.name: Phase 6: String Algorithms
phases.description: Rolling hash with randomized anti-hash hygiene, KMP pi table, Z-algorithm, Manacher, Aho-Corasick automaton, Suffix Array + LCP, and Suffix Automaton (SAM).

phases.name: Phase 7: Mathematics, Linear Algebra & Polynomials
phases.description: Linear sieve, SPF, Modular inverse, Möbius inversion, Bitwise transforms, Gaussian elimination, XOR basis, Matrix Tree Theorem, and FFT/NTT.

phases.name: Phase 8: Game Theory, Geometry & Meta-Algorithms
phases.description: Sprague-Grundy theorem, Nim, Computational geometry primitives, Monotone chain convex hull, Half-plane intersection, Meet-in-the-Middle, and Parallel BS.

tracks.name: Track A: The Core S-Tier Foundation
tracks.description: Essential high-ROI techniques that decide modern rated contests consistently. Focus on muscle memory for C++ templates and pattern recognition.

tracks.name: Track B: Candidate Master & Master Climb
tracks.description: Advanced structural decompositions, dynamic range structures, HLD, Centroid, Mo's, Dinic flow, CHT, Slope trick, and Aho-Corasick.

tracks.name: Track C: Grandmaster Mastery
tracks.description: Axiomatic matroid theory, Matroid intersection, NTT, Formal Power Series, Matrix Tree Theorem, Segment Tree Beats, LCT, and SAM.

modules.title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
modules.summary: Prefix invertible operations, binary lifting on BIT in O(log N), 2D Fenwick trees, range adds/range sums, and offline contribution counting.

topics.title: Fenwick Tree (Binary Indexed Tree)
topics.prerequisites: Prefix sums, bit tricks (`i & -i`), associative invertible ops (usually `+` / XOR)
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: S-tier
- Frequency: Very Common
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1400–2000
- Prerequisites: Prefix sums, bit tricks (`i & -i`), associative invertible ops (usually `+` / XOR)
topics.coreIntuition: Index `i` stores the sum of a contiguous block ending at `i` whose length is the lowest set bit of `i`. Walking `i += i & -i` climbs to parents for updates; walking `i -= i & -i` folds a prefix for queries. You never store “arbitrary segments” — only a canonical binary partition of prefixes — which is why Fenwick is smaller/faster than a segtree for the ops it supports.
recognitionPatterns: “Point update, prefix/range sum (or XOR)” with \(n,q \le 10^5\)–\(10^6\)
Frequency array + “how many ≤ x” after coordinate compression
Offline inversions / contribution counting with a running Fenwick
Need something lighter than a segment tree and the op has an inverse
topics.derivation:
Let \(\ell(i) = i \& -i\). Node `i` covers \((i-\ell(i), i]\).  
Prefix sum \(S(r) = \sum_{i=1}^{r} a_i\) is the sum of \(O(\log r)\) such blocks.  
Range \(S(l..r) = S(r) - S(l-1)\) needs an inverse. Update of \(a_i\) touches \(O(\log n)\) ancestors.  
**Range add, point query:** store differences \(d_i = a_i - a_{i-1}\) in a Fenwick; point \(a_i =\) prefix of \(d\).  
**Range add, range sum:** maintain two Fenwicks for \(\sum d\) and \(\sum i\cdot d\) so  
\[
\sum_{i=1}^{r} a_i = (r+1)B_1(r) - B_2(r)
\]
after range-add on \([l,r]\) updates \(B_1,B_2\) at \(l\) and \(r+1\).
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: \(O(n)\) build from array (sequential adds) or \(O(n)\) linear build
- Per-query / per-operation: \(O(\log n)\)
- Total: \(O((n+q)\log n)\) typical
- Memory: \(O(n)\)
commonBugs: 0-index vs 1-index: `i & -i` formulas assume 1-based indices
Forgetting `long long` on sums
Range sum with XOR: use `sumPrefix(r) ^ sumPrefix(l-1)`, not minus
`lower_bound` on Fenwick assumes non-negative frequencies
Off-by-one at `r+1` in range-update difference arrays when \(r=n\)
topics.variants:
- **XOR Fenwick:** same code with `^=` / `^`
- **Range update, point query:** one BIT on differences
- **Range update, range query:** `RangeBIT` above
- **2D Fenwick:** next topic
- **Fenwick on Euler tour:** subtree add / path tricks with entry-exit
- **Compression:** map values to ranks before counting
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: point updates + range sums
2. Slightly disguised: count inversions / “elements ≤ x in prefix”
3. Difficult: range add + range sum online; k-th by frequency Fenwick
4. Very difficult / advanced: Fenwick + CDQ for 3D partial order; dynamic 2D offline
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Array of size \(n\); \(q\) ops: set \(a_i \leftarrow x\) or print \(\sum_{i=l}^{r} a_i\).
2. Process updates “add \(v\) on \([l,r]\)” and queries “value at index \(i\)”.
3. Multiset of numbers in \([1,n]\); support insert/delete and “k-th smallest”.
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: invertible prefix structure + updates; prefer over segtree for sum/XOR
- Key invariant: node `i` = sum of last `i&-i` elements
- Key formula: range = prefix(r) − prefix(l−1); range-add via diffs
- Complexity: \(O(\log n)\) per op, \(O(n)\) memory
- Template to remember: `for (; i <= n; i += i & -i)` / `for (; i > 0; i -= i & -i)`

extendedTheory.overview: A Fenwick tree (Binary Indexed Tree) is a compact, cache-friendly data structure that maintains prefix sums of an array of $N$ numbers in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ space and supports $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ point updates and prefix sum queries.
keyTheorems: **Lowest Set Bit Decomposition:** For any index $i \ge 1$, $\text{LSB}(i) = i \& (-i)$. The interval managed by index $i$ in a 1-indexed BIT is $(i - \text{LSB}(i), i]$.
**Prefix Sum Invariant:** The prefix sum $S(r) = \sum_{i=1}^r A[i]$ is composed of at most $\lfloor \log_2 r \rfloor + 1$ disjoint canonical binary intervals.
**Point Update Invariant:** Incrementing $A[i]$ by $v$ propagates strictly to ancestors $i \leftarrow i + \text{LSB}(i)$, visiting at most $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ nodes.

**Binary Lifting on BIT (Order Statistics):** Finding the smallest index $r$ such that $\sum_{i=1}^r A[i] \ge k$ can be solved in pure $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time without extra binary search factors by jumping power-of-two steps from MSB to LSB.
algorithmSteps: 1. **Initialization:** Preallocate array `bit` of size $N+1$ initialized to $0$. Build in $\mathcal{O}(N)$ linear time by propagating each index $i$ to its immediate parent $i + (i \& -i)$.
2. **Point Update:** To add $v$ at index $i$: while $i \le N$, execute `bit[i] += v` and `i += i & -i`.
3. **Prefix Query:** To query $\sum_{j=1}^i A[j]$: initialize $S = 0$; while $i > 0$, execute `S += bit[i]` and `i -= i & -i`.

4. **Range Update & Range Sum:** Maintain two Fenwick trees $B_1$ and $B_2$. Adding $v$ to $[L, R]$ updates $B_1$ with $+v$ at $L$, $-v$ at $R+1$, and updates $B_2$ with $+v \cdot (L-1)$ at $L$, $-v \cdot R$ at $R+1$. The prefix sum at $r$ equals $r \cdot B_1(r) - B_2(r)$.
edgeCases: Fenwick trees MUST be 1-indexed. Passing index $0$ into $i \& -i$ causes an infinite loop ($0 \& -0 = 0$).
Coordinate compression is required when coordinates exceed $10^7$ or are negative.
Prefix sums on frequencies can exceed standard 32-bit integers; always use 64-bit `long long` for accumulators.

topics.title: 2D Fenwick Tree
topics.prerequisites: 1D Fenwick, coordinate compression, offline thinking
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: A-tier
- Frequency: Occasional
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1800–2400
- Prerequisites: 1D Fenwick, coordinate compression, offline thinking
topics.coreIntuition: Nest Fenwicks: outer index walks rows with `i & -i`, inner walks columns. Point \((x,y)\) contributes to \(O(\log X\log Y)\) nodes; rectangle prefix is inclusion-exclusion of four prefixes. True online 2D segtrees are heavier; 2D BIT + compression is the contest default for “point updates + rectangle sums.”
recognitionPatterns: Points in a plane; rectangle sum / count queries
“Add value at (x,y); query sum in \([x1,x2]\times[y1,y2]\)”
Offline 2D counting after compressing coordinates
Prefer this over naive 2D segtree when only sum/count + points matter
topics.derivation:
\[
\mathrm{pref}(X,Y)=\sum_{x\le X}\sum_{y\le Y} a_{x,y}
\]
Rectangle \([x_1,x_2]\times[y_1,y_2]\):
\[
\mathrm{pref}(x_2,y_2)-\mathrm{pref}(x_1-1,y_2)-\mathrm{pref}(x_2,y_1-1)+\mathrm{pref}(x_1-1,y_1-1).
\]
Each update/query: \(O(\log X\log Y)\). Memory \(O(XY)\) dense, or sparse maps / offline dynamic — for contests usually compress to \(\le n\).
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: \(O(1)\) empty / \(O(n\log^2)\) for \(n\) points
- Per-query / per-operation: \(O(\log X\log Y)\)
- Total: \(O(q\log^2 n)\) after compression to \(n\)
- Memory: \(O(XY)\) dense; often \(O(n^2)\) worst after compression if careless — compress both axes to ranks \(\le n\)
commonBugs: Forgetting four-term inclusion-exclusion
Using raw coordinates without compression → MLE/RE
Updating only one copy when points are “set” not “add” (subtract old value first)
Mixing 0/1-index on x and y independently
topics.variants:
- Count-only (store 1 per point)
- Offline: process by x-sweep + 1D Fenwick on y (often faster / less memory than full 2D)
- Range add rectangle + point query: 2D difference + 2D BIT
- Dynamic sparse: `map` / segment tree of Fenwicks (heavier)
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: point add, rectangle sum
2. Slightly disguised: number of points in rectangles offline
3. Difficult: rectangle add + rectangle sum (need more structure / segtree beats-style or lazy 2D — rare)
4. Very difficult / advanced: CDQ divide-conquer replacing 2D/3D structures
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. \(n\) weighted points; \(q\) axis-aligned rectangle sum queries (offline OK).
2. Grid \(n\times m\) (\(n,m\le 1000\)); point updates and sub-rectangle sums.
3. Count inversions in 2D: pairs \(i<j\), \(x_i<x_j\), \(y_i>y_j\).
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: 2D point updates + rectangle prefix sums/counts
- Key invariant: nested BIT covers
- Key formula: 4-prefix inclusion-exclusion
- Complexity: \(O(\log^2 n)\) per op after compression
- Template to remember: double `i += i & -i` loops + compress coords

modules.title: Segment Trees & Range Invariants
modules.summary: Monoid segment trees, lazy propagation tags, range assign/add, iterative bottom-up trees, segment tree beats, persistent, and dynamic trees.

topics.title: Intro to segment trees
topics.prerequisites: Arrays, associative merge ops, binary tree indexing, recursion or iterative bottom-up
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: S-tier
- Frequency: Very Common
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1400–2000
- Prerequisites: Arrays, associative merge ops, binary tree indexing, recursion or iterative bottom-up
topics.coreIntuition:
A segment tree is a complete binary tree over an array where every node stores an aggregate of a contiguous segment. Leaves are single elements; an internal node is the **merge** of its two children. The power comes from two facts:

1. Any interval `[L, R)` decomposes into **O(log n)** canonical nodes (disjoint, covering exactly the query).
2. Point/range updates touch **O(log n)** nodes if the merge is associative (and for range updates, if you add lazy — next topics).

Think less “tree of ranges” and more “**canonical cover** of intervals under a fixed partition of `[0,n)`”. The same cover idea appears in sparse tables (idempotent only), fenwick (prefix-shaped covers), and beats (canonical cover + pruning).

**When Fenwick is enough:** if you only need prefix-reducible ops (sum, XOR, or “add on point + prefix query” / “add on prefix + point query” via difference), Fenwick is shorter, faster constants, less bug surface. Reach for segtree when you need arbitrary range query + arbitrary point update for a non-prefix op (min/max with updates, GCD with updates, custom structs), or when you will grow into lazy / persistence / beats.
recognitionPatterns: “Point update + range query” or “range update + point query” with associative op → segtree/fenwick.
Op is min/max/GCD/LCM/matrix multiply/monoid struct → almost always segtree (fenwick awkward).
Need the **actual segment nodes** later (HLD, offline time-segtree, Li Chao) → learn the recursive shape even if you ship iterative.
Static array + only idempotent RMQ → sparse table wins; do not force segtree.
Online k-th / order statistics on ranges → merge-sort tree or fenwick-of-counts / PBDS, not plain sum tree unless compressed + fenwick.
topics.derivation:
Index nodes as a heap: root = 1, children `2v`, `2v+1`. For array length `n`, use size `N = next_pow2(n)` so leaves `[N, N+n)` hold values and unused leaves are identities.

**Canonical cover:** on query `[ql, qr)`:
- If node segment `[l,r)` is fully inside → take node.
- If disjoint → skip.
- Else recurse both children.
Each level contributes ≤ 2 nodes ⇒ **≤ 4⌈log₂ N⌉** nodes in the recursive formulation; iterative walks from leaves and also **O(log n)**.

**Merge must be a monoid:** associative binary op `⊕` with identity `e` (for empty / out-of-range). Commutativity not required (matrix product, string concat — careful with child order).

**Build:** `O(n)` bottom-up: leaves then `t[v] = t[2v] ⊕ t[2v+1]`.
**Point set `i ← x`:** walk leaf → root, rematerialize.
**Range query:** cover merge left-to-right (preserve order if non-commutative).

Height `⌈log₂ N⌉`, so all ops `O(log n)` time, memory `~4n` for recursive or `2N` for iterative power-of-two.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: `O(n)` build
- Per-query / per-operation: `O(log n)` point update / range query
- Total: `O((n + q) log n)` typical
- Memory: `O(n)` (~4n recursive nodes)
commonBugs: Half-open vs inclusive endpoints mismatch → off-by-one WA.
Wrong identity (`0` for min, `INF` for sum) → silent corruption.
Non-associative “merge” (e.g. mean) → wrong answers; store sum+count instead.
Updating leaf but forgetting to push merges up.
`4*n` too small when `n=1` edge; always `4*max(1,n)`.
Querying empty range without returning `e`.
Using recursive segtree on deep custom recursion + large `n` → stack overflow on some judges (prefer iterative for production).
topics.variants:
- **Point add + range sum:** fenwick preferred.
- **Range add + point query:** difference array + fenwick/segtree.
- **Store index of min:** merge keeps `(value, index)` with tie-break.
- **Walk tree for first position with property:** binary search on tree (`find_first` / `min_left` / `max_right`) — O(log n) not O(log² n).
- **Segment tree on Euler tour / HLD:** same code, different index mapping.
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: point assign, range min/sum.
2. Slightly disguised: range GCD after point updates; or “longest prefix with sum ≤ X” via tree walk.
3. Difficult: store custom monoid (max subarray sum = Kadane-on-merge with left/right/total/best).
4. Very difficult / advanced: offline queries as nodes on a time-segment tree (add edge for duration `[t1,t2)`, DSU rollback) — same skeleton, different payload.
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Array of `n` integers; `q` operations: set `a[i]=x`, or report GCD on `[l,r]`. Which structure, and why not fenwick?
2. Static array; only queries “min on `[l,r]`”, no updates. Is segtree optimal?
3. After each point update you must answer “largest `r` such that sum(`[0,r)`) ≤ `X`”. How do you avoid `O(log² n)`?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: associative range query + updates; fenwick fails (non-prefix / need walk / need lazy later).
- Key invariant: parent = merge(left, right); query = merge of O(log n) disjoint canonical nodes.
- Key formula: identity `e`, `op` associative; half-open `[l,r)`.
- Complexity: `O(n)` build, `O(log n)/op`, `O(n)` memory.
- Template to remember: recursive 4n monoid tree or iterative 2N (next topic).

extendedTheory.overview: A Segment Tree is a full binary tree designed to perform range queries and range modifications on an underlying array in $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time by maintaining monoid aggregates $(S, \oplus, e)$.
keyTheorems: **Monoid Property:** Range aggregation requires an associative binary operator $\oplus$ with an identity element $e$ such that $(a \oplus b) \oplus c = a \oplus (b \oplus c)$ and $a \oplus e = a$.
**Canonical Segment Cover:** Any arbitrary contiguous subarray $[L, R]$ is uniquely partitioned into at most $2 \lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ disjoint canonical segment tree nodes.

**Lazy Propagation Postulate:** Range updates defer evaluation to subtrees by storing pending transformation tags in ancestors, pushing them to child nodes only when deeper queries/updates traverse down.

**Segment Tree Beats Invariant:** Range $\text{chmin}(v)$ maintains the maximum and strict second maximum ($max_1, max_2$) in each node. If $max_2 < v < max_1$, the update acts as a uniform lazy subtraction on the count of maximums in $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ amortized time.
algorithmSteps: 1. **Tree Allocation:** Allocate $4N$ nodes for recursive pointers or $2N$ nodes for iterative bottom-up trees where leaves reside at indices $N \dots 2N-1$.
2. **Merge Operation:** Define `pull(node)` as `tree[node] = merge(tree[2*node], tree[2*node+1])`.

topics.title: Lazy propagation
topics.prerequisites: Segment tree monoid; composition of updates
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: S-tier
- Frequency: Very Common
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1600–2200
- Prerequisites: Segment tree monoid; composition of updates
topics.coreIntuition:
Range updates would touch `Θ(n)` leaves if applied naively. Lazy propagation stores a **pending update** on a node meaning “this update applies to the whole segment, but children are not yet materialized.” When you need to go deeper, you **push** the tag to children and clear it.

Two algebraic objects:
1. **Data monoid** `(S, ⊕, e)` — what queries return.
2. **Update monoid** `(F, ∘, id)` — how updates compose; each `f ∈ F` is an affine action on `S`: applying `f` to a node’s aggregate must be doable in `O(1)` from the tag + node length / stored aux.

Classic: range add on sum → tag `add`; `sum += add * len`. Range assign → tag `set` with priority over add. Composition order matters: usually “new update applied **after** old” or the reverse — pick one and stick to it in `compose` and `push`.
recognitionPatterns: “Add `v` on `[l,r]`, query sum/min/max on `[L,R]`” → lazy add.
“Set all on `[l,r]` to `x`, then query” → lazy assign (often with add mixed).
Updates are **uniform** on a segment and query aggregate has closed form under that update.
If updates are arbitrary per index inside range → not plain lazy; need different model.
Only range add + range sum → fenwick with difference tricks sometimes; min/max after add still wants lazy segtree.
topics.derivation:
Maintain `t[v]` = true aggregate of segment (as if all tags pushed), and `lz[v]` = pending update for children.

**Apply tag `f` to node `v` covering length `len`:**
`t[v] ← f · t[v]` (action), `lz[v] ← f ∘ lz[v]` (compose onto pending).

**Push:** if `lz[v] ≠ id`, apply `lz[v]` to both children, then `lz[v] ← id`.

**Range update on `[ql,qr)`:** same canonical descent as query; before branching, `push(v)`. On full cover, `apply` only.

**Correctness:** after every public op, root’s `t[1]` is correct; tags mean “children stale relative to parent.” Parent always reflects applied tags.

Composition associativity: `(f ∘ g) · s = f · (g · s)`.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: `O(n)`
- Per-query / per-operation: `O(log n)` amortized/worst for standard tags
- Total: `O((n+q) log n)`
- Memory: `O(n)` data + `O(n)` tags
commonBugs: Forgetting `push` before recursing → WA.
Composing tags in wrong order (assign vs add).
Applying add to min OK; applying add to sum needs `* len`.
Pushing on leaves unnecessarily / not clearing tag.
Query identity wrong when merging partials.
Mixing 0-index/1-index in `ql,qr`.
Recursion stack with lazy on large `n` (rare but real).
topics.variants:
- Add on sum / min / max / (min,max,sum) jointly.
- Affine `x ↦ a*x+b` on range with sum query (compose matrices / pairs `(a,b)`).
- Lazy on HLD paths / Euler subtours — same tags, mapped indices.
- Beats: “lazy chmin” that only sometimes fully covers — see Segment tree beats.
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard: range add, range min.
2. Slightly disguised: range add, then “count of minima” — store `(min, cnt)`.
3. Difficult: affine updates + sum; or assign+add with two-tag composition.
4. Very difficult: lazy on dynamic tree indices; or beats-style chmin.
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Ops: add `v` on `[l,r]`; query max on `[L,R]`. Fenwick or lazy segtree?
2. Ops: set every element in `[l,r]` to `x`; query sum. What tags do you need?
3. Range add on an array of matrices; query product. What must be true for lazy to work?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: uniform range updates + range queries with O(1) tag action.
- Key invariant: `t[v]` correct; `lz[v]` means children not yet updated.
- Key formula: push before descend; compose tags associatively.
- Complexity: `O(log n)` per update/query.
- Template to remember: `apply` / `push` / `pull` trio.

topics.title: Range assign/add/query
topics.prerequisites: Lazy propagation; tag composition
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: S-tier
- Frequency: Common
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1600–2200
- Prerequisites: Lazy propagation; tag composition
topics.coreIntuition:
The “kitchen sink” lazy problem: support **range assign**, **range add**, and **range sum** (often also min/max). Assign annihilates previous adds on that segment; subsequent adds apply on top of the assigned value.

Model each tag as: optional assignment `set` + additive `add`. Semantics for a value `x`:
- If `has_set`: value becomes `set + add` (or apply set then add).
- Else: `x ← x + add`.

Composition of tags `f` after `g` (first `g`, then `f`):
- If `f` has set: result = `f` (ignore `g`).
- Else: result keeps `g`’s set (if any) and `add = g.add + f.add`.

For sums: assignment sets `sum = value * len`; add does `sum += delta * len`. Same for min/max with assign/add.

This is the workhorse for AtCoder library–style problems and many CF Div.2 D/E.
recognitionPatterns: Statement lists both “paint range to x” and “increment range” plus sum/min queries.
“Reset segment then keep adding” stories (timelines, coverage with rebuild).
Need length-aware aggregates under both ops.
If only assign (no add): single set-tag suffices.
If only add: pure add-tag; don’t overbuild.
topics.derivation:
Tag `(has_set, set_val, add)` acting on node aggregate `(sum, mn, mx, len)`:

```
apply_set(v, x): sum=x*len; mn=mx=x; has_set=1; set_val=x; add=0
apply_add(v, d): sum+=d*len; mn+=d; mx+=d; add+=d  (set_val+=d if has_set)
```

Composition `f ∘ g` (g first):
```
if f.has_set: return f
else: g.add += f.add; if g.has_set: g.set_val += f.add; return g
```

Push applies tag to children then clears. Pull merges children sums/mins/maxes.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: `O(n)`
- Per-query / per-operation: `O(log n)`
- Total: `O((n+q) log n)`
- Memory: `O(n)`
commonBugs: Assign not clearing pending add (or vice versa).
Double-counting: set tag stores `set_val` and also `add` inconsistently.
`len` wrong on partial nodes after bad pull.
Composition: “new set should wipe old add” forgotten → WA on mixed ops.
Min/max not updated on add.
Using int for sum when `x * len` overflows → use `int64`.
topics.variants:
- Assign + sum only.
- Assign + add + min/max/sum (full).
- Affine `a*x+b` with composition `(a1,b1)∘(a2,b2)=(a1*a2, a1*b2+b1)`.
- Modulo arithmetic on sums.
- History: persistent lazy is rarely needed; usually offline or beats instead.
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard: paint / increment / sum.
2. Slightly disguised: “set range to 0 then add 1 on subranges” coverage rebuilds.
3. Difficult: maintain sum of `f(a_i)` under assign/add when `f` is polynomial — store power sums.
4. Very difficult: assign/add plus chmin (forces beats or casesplit).
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Support range set, range add, range sum. Sketch tag composition when set follows add.
2. Same ops but query “number of zeros in range”. What extra info do nodes store under assign/add?
3. Only range set + range sum — can you use a fenwick? When yes/no?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: mixed paint + increment + aggregates.
- Key invariant: set dominates; add stacks; `sum`/`mn`/`mx` always consistent with tags.
- Key formula: set ⇒ `sum=x*len`; add ⇒ `sum+=d*len`.
- Complexity: `O(log n)` per op.
- Template to remember: two-field tag `(set?, add)` with wipe-on-set.

topics.title: Iterative segment tree
topics.prerequisites: Monoid segment tree idea; bit tricks helpful
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: A-tier
- Frequency: Common
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1400–2000
- Prerequisites: Monoid segment tree idea; bit tricks helpful
topics.coreIntuition:
Pad `n` to `N = 2^{⌈log2 n⌉}` (or use non-pow2 size carefully). Store leaves at `[N, N+n)`, parents at `i>>1`. Point updates climb parents. Range queries walk from `l+=N`, `r+=N` toward root, consuming complete segments when endpoints are odd/even — **no recursion, no lazy in the classic form**.

Why contestants love it: ~2× less constant than recursive, no stack, tiny code for point-update range-query. Why not always: classic iterative form does **not** support lazy range updates cleanly (possible but ugly); non-commutative ops need careful left/right accumulation; find-first walks differ slightly.

**Vs recursive:** same asymptotics; iterative wins on TL; recursive wins on clarity for lazy / beats / persistence / dynamic nodes.
recognitionPatterns: Point update + range query only → iterative is default ship choice.
Need maximum speed for monoid queries in HLD (many segops) → iterative.
Lazy / assign → stay recursive (or specialized).
Non-commutative merge → must merge `left_acc = op(node, left_acc)` vs `right_acc = op(right_acc, node)` correctly.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: `O(n)` after padding
- Per-query / per-operation: `O(log n)`
- Total: `O((n+q) log n)`
- Memory: `O(N) = O(n)`
commonBugs: Forgetting to pad / using `n` not `N` as leaf base.
Non-commutative: swapping `L`/`R` combine order.
Inclusive `r` passed into half-open API.
`max_right`/`min_left` bit conditions wrong (`l & -l`).
Building without initializing unused leaves to `e`.
topics.variants:
- Non-power-of-two size with `size = n` leaves at `size` and parents still `i/2` (AtCoder style) — works if `query` same.
- Dual fenwick-like for only invertible ops — not general.
- Iterative lazy exists (segment tree beats blogs) but rarely worth vs recursive.
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard: point set, range min/sum.
2. Slightly disguised: HLD path aggregates with many queries.
3. Difficult: `max_right` for first prefix failing a predicate.
4. Very difficult: combine with Mo / offline — usually overkill vs recursive clarity.
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Point updates, range products modulo prime. Iterative or fenwick?
2. You need range add later in the same problem. Start iterative or recursive?
3. Non-commutative matrix product on ranges, point set. What must query preserve?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: point update + range query; speed/clarity without lazy.
- Key invariant: `t[i] = op(t[2i], t[2i+1])`; leaves at `N+i`.
- Key formula: while-loop odd-endpoint consumption.
- Complexity: `O(log n)`, memory `2N`.
- Template to remember: AtCoder-style iterative monoid tree.

topics.title: Segment tree beats
topics.prerequisites: Lazy segtree fluency; chmin/chmax intuition; amortized analysis comfort
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: Niche
- Frequency: Rare
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 2400–3200
- Prerequisites: Lazy segtree fluency; chmin/chmax intuition; amortized analysis comfort
topics.coreIntuition:
Classic lazy fails for **range chmin** (`a_i ← min(a_i, x)`) because the update is not a uniform affine tag on arbitrary child values — unless the whole segment’s maximum is `≤ x` (tag is no-op) or you know enough structure to update aggregates in O(1).

**Beats** stores at each node: `mx`, `se` (strict second max), `mx_cnt`, often `sum`, and maybe `mn`/`se_min` for chmax. On chmin(`x`):
- If `mx ≤ x`: break (nothing changes).
- If `se < x < mx`: you can **beat** the node — only the maximums drop to `x`; update `sum`, `mx`, tags; **do not descend**.
- Else (`x ≤ se`): must push and recurse both children.

Amortized potential on “number of distinct values / tight maxima” gives **O(log² n)** per op typical (sometimes O(log n) amortized depending on proof). Extremely powerful on the right problem; **terrible early ROI** — learn after lazy mastery, ignore until ~2400+.
recognitionPatterns: Range `a_i = min(a_i, x)` / `max(a_i, x)` plus sum or max queries.
“Cap all values in range above threshold” repeatedly.
Not plain assign/add; not invertible fenwick.
If offline and only chmin + sum, sometimes CDQ / divide-conquer on time beats beats — consider alternatives first.
topics.derivation:
Node invariants: `mx` = maximum; `se` = max among strictly `< mx` (or `-inf`); `cnt` = count of `mx`.

Chmin tag `x` when `se < x < mx`:
```
sum -= (mx - x) * cnt
mx = x
```
Push chmin to children with same rules.

Potential Φ = Σ_nodes (number of “distinct maximum chains”) — each failed beat (recurse) decreases global potential enough to amortize. Practical bound used in contests: treat as `O(log² n)` per update/query.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: `O(n)`
- Per-query / per-operation: amortized `O(log² n)` typical for chmin/chmax/add/sum suite
- Total: ~`O(q log² n)` 
- Memory: `O(n)` with large constant (~10–20 fields/node)
commonBugs: Wrong second-max after partial beat.
Not handling all-equal segment (`se = -inf`) when chmin collapses.
Forgetting to push add before chmin tags (tag order).
Using beats when assign would suffice.
TLE from missing break `mx ≤ x` → descends like O(n).
topics.variants:
- Chmin + sum only (lighter node).
- Chmin + chmax + add + sum (full “beats”).
- Historic beats on CF (jiupeng / angel) tutorials — stick to one verified template.
- Alternative: sqrt decomposition on values for some chmin problems.
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: range chmin, query sum.
2. Slightly disguised: repeatedly replace `a_i` with `min(a_i, x)` offline online mix.
3. Difficult: chmin/chmax/add together with max and sum queries.
4. Very difficult / advanced: beats on trees via HLD (constants brutal).
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Range operation `a_i ← min(a_i, x)`, query sum. Why classic lazy assign fails?
2. Same problem offline with all `x` known — name one alternative to beats.
3. Node stores `mx` but not `se`. Can you still beat in O(1) on a full cover?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: range chmin/chmax (+ add/sum) when forced online; else consider offline.
- Key invariant: second extremum enables O(1) partial update when only maxima change.
- Key formula: if `se < x < mx`, drop maxima to `x` and stop.
- Complexity: amortized ~`O(log² n)`.
- Template to remember: break / beat / recurse trichotomy + push order add→chmin→chmax.

4. **Range Query:** If current node interval $[l, r] \subseteq [L, R]$, return `tree[node]`. If $[l, r] \cap [L, R] = \emptyset$, return identity $e$. Otherwise push lazy tag, split query at $mid$, and merge child results.
edgeCases: Ensure lazy tag composition is strictly associative: when assigning and adding, assignment overrides pending addition.
For Range Assign, lazy tag empty state cannot be $0$ if $0$ is a valid value; use an explicit `has_lazy` boolean flag or $-1$/infinity sentinel.
Iterative segment trees require $1$-based indexing and powers-of-two padding when performing non-commutative queries.

topics.title: Persistent segment tree
topics.prerequisites: Segtree; path-copying persistence; coordinate compression
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: A-tier
- Frequency: Occasional
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1900–2600
- Prerequisites: Segtree; path-copying persistence; coordinate compression
topics.coreIntuition:
Each update creates a **new root**; unchanged subtrees are **shared**. An update copies `O(log n)` nodes. You keep `roots[0..q]` representing versions of the array / frequency tree.

Killer application: **k-th smallest on `[L,R]`** — build persistent frequency tree over compressed values, version `i` = after inserting `a[0..i)`. Then k-th on `[L,R]` = walk on `roots[R] - roots[L]` (subtract counts on the fly) in `O(log V)`.

**Vs merge-sort tree:** persistent usually less memory (`O((n+q) log V)` nodes vs `O(n log n)` full vectors), faster k-th, supports “versions.” Merge-sort tree easier for arbitrary `[lo,hi]` counts without thinking in roots.

**Vs Mo + fenwick:** Mo is offline only; persistent is online-friendly for prefix versions.
recognitionPatterns: K-th in subarray `[L,R]` (static).
“How array looked after update `t`” queries.
Count of values in `[a,b]` on `[L,R]` via version difference.
Functional graph / DFS timestamps with historical queries.
Need true mutable persistence with range lazy — rare and hard; usually avoid.
topics.derivation:
Node `{left_ptr, right_ptr, sum}`. Update at leaf index `p` (value coord):
```
new_node = copy(old)
if leaf: sum += delta
else: recurse to child, replace child ptr with new child, sum = L.sum+R.sum
```
`O(log V)` new nodes per update.

Query k-th between two roots `u,v` (v = right prefix, u = left prefix):
```
walk from top:
  left_cnt = v.left.sum - u.left.sum
  if k < left_cnt: go left
  else: k -= left_cnt; go right
```

Space: `O(n log V)` for n insertions.
topics.templatePython:
# Educational only — expect TLE/MLE on tight CF
class Persist:
    __slots__ = ("N", "l", "r", "s", "roots")

    def __init__(self, N: int):
        self.N = N
        self.l = [0]
        self.r = [0]
        self.s = [0]
        self.roots = [0]

    def _copy(self, v):
        self.l.append(self.l[v])
        self.r.append(self.r[v])
        self.s.append(self.s[v])
        return len(self.s) - 1

    def _add(self, v, L, R, pos, delta):
        v = self._copy(v)
        self.s[v] += delta
        if R - L == 1:
            return v
        m = (L + R) // 2
        if pos < m:
            self.l[v] = self._add(self.l[v], L, m, pos, delta)
        else:
            self.r[v] = self._add(self.r[v], m, R, pos, delta)
        return v

    def upd(self, root, pos, delta):
        nr = self._add(root, 0, self.N, pos, delta)
        self.roots.append(nr)
        return nr
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: `O(n log V)` to insert n points
- Per-query / per-operation: `O(log V)` update or k-th / range count
- Total: `O((n+q) log V)`
- Memory: `O((n+q) log V)` nodes (~2 ints + sum each)
commonBugs: Forgetting compression; `N` too large → MLE.
Using `roots[R]-roots[L-1]` indexing off-by-one on half-open.
Not reserving vector capacity → slow realloc.
Recursing with null child `0` incorrectly (ensure `t[0]` is empty identity).
Persistent **lazy** without care → exponential copies; avoid unless expert.
topics.variants:
- Persistent on index axis with point set (historical arrays).
- Persistent + segment tree on time for rollback-like queries.
- Chairman tree = persistent frequency tree nickname.
- Fully persistent vs partial (only update latest) — contests almost always partial.
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: k-th smallest in `[L,R]`.
2. Slightly disguised: count distinct in `[L,R]` with last-occurrence persistent trick.
3. Difficult: persistent + HLD / trees.
4. Very difficult / advanced: persistent Li Chao; persistent lazy (rare).
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Static `a[1..n]`; query k-th in `[L,R]`. Merge-sort tree vs persistent — tradeoffs?
2. After each update you must answer queries on **past** versions. Which property do you need?
3. Count values in `[x,y]` on index `[L,R]` with persistent freq tree — how, in one walk?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: versions / k-th on subarrays / rectangle counts via roots.
- Key invariant: path copy O(log); shared unchanged subtrees.
- Key formula: `kth(roots[L], roots[R], k)` on value tree.
- Complexity: `O(log V)` per op, `O(n log V)` memory.
- Template to remember: node pool + copy-on-write add.

extendedTheory.overview: A Segment Tree is a full binary tree designed to perform range queries and range modifications on an underlying array in $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time by maintaining monoid aggregates $(S, \oplus, e)$.
keyTheorems: **Monoid Property:** Range aggregation requires an associative binary operator $\oplus$ with an identity element $e$ such that $(a \oplus b) \oplus c = a \oplus (b \oplus c)$ and $a \oplus e = a$.
**Canonical Segment Cover:** Any arbitrary contiguous subarray $[L, R]$ is uniquely partitioned into at most $2 \lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ disjoint canonical segment tree nodes.

**Lazy Propagation Postulate:** Range updates defer evaluation to subtrees by storing pending transformation tags in ancestors, pushing them to child nodes only when deeper queries/updates traverse down.

**Segment Tree Beats Invariant:** Range $\text{chmin}(v)$ maintains the maximum and strict second maximum ($max_1, max_2$) in each node. If $max_2 < v < max_1$, the update acts as a uniform lazy subtraction on the count of maximums in $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ amortized time.
algorithmSteps: 1. **Tree Allocation:** Allocate $4N$ nodes for recursive pointers or $2N$ nodes for iterative bottom-up trees where leaves reside at indices $N \dots 2N-1$.
2. **Merge Operation:** Define `pull(node)` as `tree[node] = merge(tree[2*node], tree[2*node+1])`.
3. **Pushing Lazy Tags:** Before traversing into children of `node`, apply `tree[node].lazy` to `2*node` and `2*node+1`, then clear `tree[node].lazy`.

4. **Range Query:** If current node interval $[l, r] \subseteq [L, R]$, return `tree[node]`. If $[l, r] \cap [L, R] = \emptyset$, return identity $e$. Otherwise push lazy tag, split query at $mid$, and merge child results.
edgeCases: Ensure lazy tag composition is strictly associative: when assigning and adding, assignment overrides pending addition.
For Range Assign, lazy tag empty state cannot be $0$ if $0$ is a valid value; use an explicit `has_lazy` boolean flag or $-1$/infinity sentinel.
Iterative segment trees require $1$-based indexing and powers-of-two padding when performing non-commutative queries.

topics.title: Dynamic segment tree
topics.prerequisites: Segtree; pointers/indices pool; coordinate ranges up to 1e9/1e18
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: B-tier
- Frequency: Occasional
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 2000–2600
- Prerequisites: Segtree; pointers/indices pool; coordinate ranges up to 1e9/1e18
topics.coreIntuition:
When the index universe is huge (`[1, 1e18]`) but you only touch `q` positions/segments, allocate nodes **on demand**. Same recursive logic; children start null. Memory `O(q log U)` not `O(U)`.

**Vs compression:** if all coordinates known offline, **compress to 1..m** and use dense segtree/fenwick — simpler and faster. Dynamic wins when online (coordinates appear live) or when compression awkward (ranges as indices with splits).

**Vs fenwick:** fenwick needs dense 1..n; dynamic segtree is the sparse analogue for arbitrary associative ops / lazy on large universe.
recognitionPatterns: Indices up to `1e9`/`1e18`, only `q ≤ 1e5` updates.
Online coordinates; cannot compress ahead.
Range add/sum on huge line (coverage of segments).
“Implicit segtree” / “sparse segtree” wording in blogs.
topics.derivation:
Each node covers `[l,r]` mid `(l+r)/2` carefully with `int128` or `long long` mid to avoid overflow: `m = l + (r-l)/2`.

On update, if node null create it. Descend only needed side(s). Query skips null (treat as identity).

With lazy: store tag on sparse node; push creates children if needed.

Node count: each update creates ≤ `2 log U` new nodes worst case.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: `O(1)` empty tree
- Per-query / per-operation: `O(log U)` time; `O(log U)` new nodes per update worst-case
- Total: `O(q log U)`
- Memory: `O(q log U)`
commonBugs: Mid overflow: `(l+r)/2` for `l,r ~ 1e18` → use `l + (r-l)/2`.
Inclusive vs half-open confusion on huge ranges.
Forgetting to create children on push with lazy.
Using dynamic when offline compression would be trivial.
MLE from not reserving / leaking nodes on wrong recursion.
topics.variants:
- Point update / range query sparse.
- Lazy range add / range sum on `[1,1e18]`.
- Dynamic on two axes → “2D dynamic” (next topic) — usually prefer alternatives.
- Persistent + dynamic combined (node pool versions).
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: range coverage on coordinate line `1e9`.
2. Slightly disguised: store segments as +1/-1 on compressed ends — sometimes fenwick enough.
3. Difficult: dynamic lazy + walking for first true predicate.
4. Very difficult / advanced: dynamic Li Chao on `1e18` x-axis.
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Online: add point `(x,v)` with `x∈[1,1e18]`; query sum on `[L,R]`. Compress or dynamic?
2. All `x` given in input before queries. Preferred approach?
3. Range add on `[L,R] ⊆ [1,1e18]`, query point. Difference array ideas vs dynamic lazy?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: huge universe, few touches, especially online.
- Key invariant: null child = identity segment; allocate on write.
- Key formula: mid = `l+(r-l)/2`; memory `O(q log U)`.
- Complexity: `O(log U)` per op.
- Template to remember: index pool with `L,R` child ints + lazy optional.

topics.title: 2D segment tree / alternatives
topics.prerequisites: Segtree; 2D fenwick; CDQ divide-conquer; offline thinking
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: C-tier
- Frequency: Rare
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 2200–2800
- Prerequisites: Segtree; 2D fenwick; CDQ divide-conquer; offline thinking
topics.coreIntuition:
Naive 2D segtree: segtree on `x`, each node holds a segtree on `y` of points in that `x`-segment. Build/memory `O(n log² n)` for points; query rectangle `O(log² n)`; updates painful.

**Early ROI is low** because almost every “2D range” CF problem has a better tool:
- **2D fenwick** on compressed grid — if point add + rectangle sum.
- **CDQ / D&C on time** — offline 3D partial order.
- **Sweep + 1D fenwick/segtree** — classic.
- **Merge-sort tree** — static `x` as index, `y` as value.
- **Persistent segtree** — insert by `x`, query `y`-range on version difference.

Use true 2D segtree only when online 2D with ops that don’t fit fenwick and offline is impossible.
recognitionPatterns: Rectangle sum with point updates on grid → 2D fenwick first.
Offline “add point / query rectangle” → sweep or CDQ.
Static points, query count in rectangle → merge-sort / persistent / fenwick2D build.
Online arbitrary 2D range chmin — suffering; rethink problem.
topics.derivation:
For `n` points: outer tree sorts by `x` (or builds on compressed `x`). Node’s inner structure stores all points with that `x`-range sorted by `y` (merge-sort style) or a balanced BST/fenwick of `y`.

Rectangle query `[x1,x2] × [y1,y2]`: O(log n) outer nodes × O(log n) inner = O(log² n).

Memory: if each outer node stores fenwick of size = points in node, total `O(n log n)`.

Segment-of-segment-of-arrays without care → `O(n log² n)` memory easy MLE.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: 2D fenwick `O(nm)` or `O(n log² n)` sparse builds; naive 2D seg `O(n log² n)`
- Per-query / per-operation: `O(log² n)` typical rectangle
- Total: depends; CDQ often `O(n log² n)` offline
- Memory: fenwick2D dense `O(nm)`; sparse `O(n log n)` — 2D seg easy MLE
commonBugs: Reaching for 2D segtree when 2D fenwick suffices.
MLE from `vector` of full inner trees sized to global `m`.
Off-by-one in rectangle inclusion-exclusion.
Compressing x/y inconsistently between updates and queries.
Online 2D with deletes without invertible op → stuck.
topics.variants:
- 2D fenwick (invertible).
- Segtree of fenwicks / fenwick of segtrees.
- Persistent segtree as 2D count.
- CDQ for 3-sided/4-sided offline.
- Quadtrees (rare in CF).
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: point add, rectangle sum → 2D fenwick.
2. Slightly disguised: static points rectangle count → compress + fenwick2D or merge-sort tree.
3. Difficult: online 2D with set (non-invertible) — seg of policy BST.
4. Very difficult / advanced: 2D lazy — almost never; reformulate.
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. `n≤2000` grid, point add, rectangle sum. Best structure?
2. `n≤1e5` static points, many rectangle counts. List two approaches that beat naive 2D segtree coding time.
3. Offline: add point, query “points with `x≤X, y≤Y, time≤T`”. Name the technique family.
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: only if simpler 2D fenwick / sweep / CDQ / persistent fail.
- Key invariant: outer canonical x-nodes × inner y-structure.
- Key formula: rectangle = inclusion-exclusion on 2D prefixes when invertible.
- Complexity: usually `O(log² n)` query; watch memory.
- Template to remember: **prefer fenwick2D**; seg-of-fenwicks if forced dynamic.

topics.title: When each variant is actually useful
topics.frequency: Very Common (every segtree problem is a choice)
topics.prerequisites: Exposure to the variants above; fenwick fluency
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: S-tier (as decision skill)
- Frequency: Very Common (every segtree problem is a choice)
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1400–2800
- Prerequisites: Exposure to the variants above; fenwick fluency
topics.coreIntuition:
The highest-ROI skill is **not** coding beats — it is picking the lightest structure that fits:

| Need | First reach |
|------|-------------|
| Point add + prefix/range sum | Fenwick |
| Point set + range min/max/GCD | Iterative segtree |
| Range add + range min/sum | Lazy segtree |
| Range set + add + sum | Assign/add lazy |
| Range chmin + sum online | Beats (or offline alt) |
| K-th in subarray static | Persistent / wavelet / MST |
| Huge index universe online | Dynamic segtree |
| Rectangle sum invertible | 2D fenwick / sweep |
| Historical versions | Persistent |

Wrong choice costs more than wrong constant factor.
recognitionPatterns: Ask: invertible? offline? static? need lazy? need 2D? need order-stat?
If yes to invertible prefix → fenwick.
If idempotent static RMQ → sparse table.
If only “subarray k-th” → persistent, not general lazy.
If chmin → confirm online necessity before beats.
topics.derivation:
Decision tree (contest speed):
1. No updates → sparse table / prefix / sort + BS.
2. Updates but prefix-shaped → fenwick (± difference).
3. Point update, range monoid → iterative segtree.
4. Range update uniform → lazy; classify add vs set vs affine vs chmin.
5. Value-index 2D static → MST / persistent / fenwick2D.
6. Versions → persistent.
7. Universe huge online → dynamic.
8. True online 2D non-invertible → rare heavy artillery.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: N/A (decision O(1) with practice)
- Per-query / per-operation: whatever chosen structure
- Total: minimizing implement + debug time is the real objective
- Memory: prefer `O(n)` fenwick/iterative over `O(n log n)` MST when possible
commonBugs: Implementing lazy when fenwick difference works.
Beats for a problem that is offline-friendly.
2D segtree as first idea → MLE/TLE/code bomb.
Persistent when Mo + fenwick is enough offline.
Dynamic when all coords offline-compressible.
topics.variants: - ICPC team: one member owns “lazy kitchen sink,” another “persistent k-th,” another “offline CDQ” — divide recognition.
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: read ops list → classify into table row.
2. Slightly disguised: tree path queries → HLD + (usually iterative/lazy) seg.
3. Difficult: mix version queries + range updates → rethink (often offline).
4. Very difficult / advanced: force beats + HLD — check constraints twice.
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Ops: range add, point query. Lightest tool?
2. Ops: point set, range matrix product. Why fenwick fails?
3. Ops: range chmin, range sum, `n=1e5`, online. What do you implement at 2600 vs at 1800 (alternative)?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: every time before coding a segtree.
- Key invariant: lightest correct tool wins.
- Key formula: fenwick ⊂ iterative ⊂ lazy ⊂ beats; MST ≈ persistent for static order-stat; 2D fenwick ≫ 2D seg.
- Complexity: pick structure whose complexity matches constraints with room.
- Template to remember: the decision table in B.

2. **Merge Operation:** Define `pull(node)` as `tree[node] = merge(tree[2*node], tree[2*node+1])`.
3. **Pushing Lazy Tags:** Before traversing into children of `node`, apply `tree[node].lazy` to `2*node` and `2*node+1`, then clear `tree[node].lazy`.

4. **Range Query:** If current node interval $[l, r] \subseteq [L, R]$, return `tree[node]`. If $[l, r] \cap [L, R] = \emptyset$, return identity $e$. Otherwise push lazy tag, split query at $mid$, and merge child results.

For Range Assign, lazy tag empty state cannot be $0$ if $0$ is a valid value; use an explicit `has_lazy` boolean flag or $-1$/infinity sentinel.
Iterative segment trees require $1$-based indexing and powers-of-two padding when performing non-commutative queries.

topics.coreIntuition:
CF does not say “use a segment tree.” It says:

Pattern library (recognition → structure):

2. **Kadane monoid** — max subarray under point updates.
3. **First position / walking** — `max_right` on sums or mins.
4. **Difference + fenwick** disguised as range add.
5. **Time-segment tree + DSU rollback** — offline dynamic connectivity.
6. **Persistent k-th** — “mex / k-th / count ≤x on subarray.”
7. **Lazy assign colors** — paint subarrays, query sums of values.
8. **Merge-sort tree** — static 2D count on array indices.
9. **Li Chao** (segtree of lines) — DP CHT geometric; related family.
10. **Beats** — rare Div.1 chmin statements.
recognitionPatterns: “Subtree of rooted tree” → Euler `[in,out)` + fenwick/segtree.
“Path u–v” → HLD or Euler+LCA tricks depending on op.
“Delete edges for a period, answer connectivity” → time segtree.
“K-th favorite number in range” → persistent.
“Replace all >x by x on range” → beats keyword.
Multiple paints of entire ranges → lazy set.
topics.derivation:
Map statement nouns to axes:
- **Index axis** (array position / Euler time / HLD position)
- **Value axis** (compressed for order-stat)
- **Time axis** (versions / offline segments)

Most CF segtree problems are 1–2 axes. Three axes → CDQ or heavy 2D.

Complexity target: usually `O((n+q) log n)` or `log²`; `log³` risky at 1e5 unless light.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: tour `O(n)`; HLD `O(n)`; structure as usual
- Per-query / per-operation: `O(log n)` to `O(log² n)` typical CF
- Total: design for `≤ 2e5` ops × `log`/`log²`
- Memory: stay within 256MB — avoid `O(n log n)` vectors unless needed

HLD wrong `op` order on path (non-commutative).

extendedTheory.overview: A Segment Tree is a full binary tree designed to perform range queries and range modifications on an underlying array in $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time by maintaining monoid aggregates $(S, \oplus, e)$.
keyTheorems: **Monoid Property:** Range aggregation requires an associative binary operator $\oplus$ with an identity element $e$ such that $(a \oplus b) \oplus c = a \oplus (b \oplus c)$ and $a \oplus e = a$.
**Canonical Segment Cover:** Any arbitrary contiguous subarray $[L, R]$ is uniquely partitioned into at most $2 \lceil \log_2 N \rceil$ disjoint canonical segment tree nodes.

**Lazy Propagation Postulate:** Range updates defer evaluation to subtrees by storing pending transformation tags in ancestors, pushing them to child nodes only when deeper queries/updates traverse down.

**Segment Tree Beats Invariant:** Range $\text{chmin}(v)$ maintains the maximum and strict second maximum ($max_1, max_2$) in each node. If $max_2 < v < max_1$, the update acts as a uniform lazy subtraction on the count of maximums in $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ amortized time.
algorithmSteps: 1. **Tree Allocation:** Allocate $4N$ nodes for recursive pointers or $2N$ nodes for iterative bottom-up trees where leaves reside at indices $N \dots 2N-1$.
2. **Merge Operation:** Define `pull(node)` as `tree[node] = merge(tree[2*node], tree[2*node+1])`.
3. **Pushing Lazy Tags:** Before traversing into children of `node`, apply `tree[node].lazy` to `2*node` and `2*node+1`, then clear `tree[node].lazy`.

4. **Range Query:** If current node interval $[l, r] \subseteq [L, R]$, return `tree[node]`. If $[l, r] \cap [L, R] = \emptyset$, return identity $e$. Otherwise push lazy tag, split query at $mid$, and merge child results.
edgeCases: Ensure lazy tag composition is strictly associative: when assigning and adding, assignment overrides pending addition.
For Range Assign, lazy tag empty state cannot be $0$ if $0$ is a valid value; use an explicit `has_lazy` boolean flag or $-1$/infinity sentinel.
Iterative segment trees require $1$-based indexing and powers-of-two padding when performing non-commutative queries.

topics.title: Merge sort tree
topics.prerequisites: Segment tree structure; binary search; sorted vectors; fenwick/PBDS alternatives awareness
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: B-tier
- Frequency: Occasional
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1800–2400
- Prerequisites: Segment tree structure; binary search; sorted vectors; fenwick/PBDS alternatives awareness
topics.coreIntuition:
Each segtree node stores the **multiset of values** in its segment, usually as a **sorted vector** (static) or fenwick/policy BST (dynamic). Build merges child vectors like merge-sort — hence the name.

Query “how many values in `[L,R]` are `≤ x`” = sum over O(log n) nodes of `upper_bound` in each sorted vector → **O(log² n)**.

**Vs persistent segtree:** merge-sort tree is simpler for static arrays; updates are painful (need fenwick-in-nodes or rebuild). Persistent / fenwick-on-compressed-values often better for “k-th in range” with updates or for online versions.

**Vs fenwick of counts:** if coordinates compressed and you only need global order-stat, fenwick wins. Merge-sort tree shines for **range + value** 2D constraints on a static array.
recognitionPatterns: Static array; queries: count of elements in `[L,R]` with value in `[a,b]`.
K-th smallest in subarray (static) — also wavelet / persistent; merge-sort tree is the “first idea.”
“Number of inversions where …” offline with range structures.
Updates present → prefer BIT of BITs, dynamic segtree, or policy PBDS + fenwick, not classic merge-sort tree.
topics.derivation:
Build: leaf `{a[i]}`; parent = merge(left_sorted, right_sorted) in linear time → total `O(n log n)` time and memory (each element appears in `O(log n)` nodes).

Count `≤ x` on `[ql,qr)`:
```
ans = 0
descend canonical nodes; ans += upper_bound(node.vec, x) - begin
```
Each of `O(log n)` nodes costs `O(log n)` binary search ⇒ `O(log² n)`.

K-th in range: binary search value `mid` counting ≤ mid, or walk tree comparing left-node counts (wavelet-style) for `O(log² n)`.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: `O(n log n)` time and memory
- Per-query / per-operation: `O(log² n)` count; k-th `O(log³ n)` if binary search + count, or `O(log² n)` with tree walk on values
- Total: `O(n log n + q log² n)`
- Memory: `O(n log n)`
commonBugs: Using `merge` incorrectly / not sorting leaves.
Memory MLE at `n=1e6` (`n log n` ints).
Updates attempted on immutable vectors.
Off-by-one in `lower_bound`/`upper_bound` for inclusive `hi`.
k-th binary search on wrong value domain (must compress or use true min/max).
topics.variants:
- Fenwick/segtree of sorted lists with updates via BITs in nodes (heavy).
- Wavelet tree: similar queries, often faster constants, harder to code.
- Persistent segtree on value axis: better for k-th + updates via path copy.
- Mo’s algorithm + fenwick: alternative for some range frequency queries.
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: count values in `[a,b]` on index range `[L,R]`.
2. Slightly disguised: number of pairs `i<j` in range with `a_i>a_j` offline.
3. Difficult: distinct values count — merge-sort tree alone insufficient; need other tricks (Mo, Hilbert, persistent + DSU).
4. Very difficult / advanced: with updates — migrate to dynamic/persistent structures.
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Static array; `q` queries: how many `a_i ∈ [L,R]` have `a_i ≤ x`. Structure?
2. Same but point updates change `a_i`. Why is classic merge-sort tree a bad fit?
3. Only need global k-th after insertions (no index range). Merge-sort tree or fenwick/PBDS?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: static array; range + value rectangle counts.
- Key invariant: node vector = sorted multiset of segment.
- Key formula: count = Σ `upper-lower` over O(log n) nodes.
- Complexity: build `O(n log n)`, query `O(log² n)`, memory `O(n log n)`.
- Template to remember: merge children vectors; binary search per node.

extendedTheory.overview: A Merge Sort Tree stores a sorted array of elements at each segment tree node, enabling static 2D range frequency queries (e.g., counting values in $[X_1, X_2]$ within index range $[L, R]$) in $\mathcal{O}(\log^2 N)$ time, or $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ using Fractional Cascading.
keyTheorems: **Space Complexity:** Built in $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ time and $\mathcal{O}(N \log N)$ space, since each level of the segment tree stores exactly $N$ elements across all nodes.

**Fractional Cascading Acceleration:** By precomputing pointers from each parent vector element to its lower-bound position in the left and right child vectors, binary search is executed only once at the root in $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$, reducing total query time from $\mathcal{O}(\log^2 N)$ to $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$.
algorithmSteps: 1. **Build:** For leaf node $i$, `tree[node] = {A[i]}`. For internal nodes, merge sorted vectors of children using `std::merge`.
2. **Fractional Cascading Pointers:** For each element in `tree[node]`, record `to_left = lower_bound(tree[2*node])` and `to_right = lower_bound(tree[2*node+1])`.
3. **Range Count Query:** Decompose $[L, R]$ into $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ canonical nodes. In each node, evaluate `upper_bound(X2) - lower_bound(X1)`.
edgeCases: Merge sort trees are static; point updates require 2D segment trees or Fenwick trees with coordinate compression.
For dynamic $k$-th queries with updates, prefer a Persistent Segment Tree or PBDS Treap over Merge Sort Trees.

modules.summary: Block decomposition, range updates with O(sqrt(N)) blocks, Mo's algorithm on arrays in O((N+Q)sqrt(N)), Hilbert curve sorting, and Mo's on trees.

topics.title: Mo's algorithm
topics.prerequisites: Offline queries, block ordering, frequency maps
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: B-tier
- Frequency: Occasional
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1900–2500
- Prerequisites: Offline queries, block ordering, frequency maps
topics.coreIntuition: Mo answers many range queries on a **static** array by physically moving a sliding window \([cl,cr]\) to each query’s \([l,r]\), applying `add`/`del` at the endpoints. Sorting queries in **blocks** (by \(l/\mathrm{B}\), then by \(r\)) makes total movement \(O(n\sqrt q)\) (or \(O(n\sqrt n)\)). Prefer Mo when **maintaining the answer under ± one endpoint** is easy, but building a mergeable segment-tree node for the same answer is painful (distinct count with fancy secondary stats, mode, XOR basis size, etc.). Prefer a **segtree** when you need updates or online answers — see comparison in the [section index](18-randomization-misc.md).
recognitionPatterns: Offline \([l,r]\) queries, array immutable
“Number of distinct”, “frequency of mode”, “count values with freq > 0 satisfying P”
Add/del an index updates a global frequency structure in \(O(1)\) or \(O(\log)\)
Segtree merge would need sets/maps in each node → TLE/MLE
topics.derivation:
Block size \(B \approx n / \sqrt{q}\) (or \(\sqrt n\)).
Sort: key `(l/B, r)` (odd blocks can reverse \(r\) — Hilbert/improving constant).
Across \(q\) queries: \(l\) moves \(O(B)\) within a block × \(q\) plus \(O(n/B)\) block changes × \(n\) → with \(B\sim n/\sqrt{q}\), total endpoint moves \(O(n\sqrt{q})\).
Time \(O((n\sqrt{q})\cdot F)\) for add/del cost \(F\).
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: compress + sort queries \(O((n+q)\log n)\)
- Per-query / per-operation: amortized via total moves
- Total: \(O((n+q)\sqrt{n}\cdot F)\) typical with \(F=O(1)\)
- Memory: \(O(n+q + \sigma)\) for frequencies
commonBugs: Wrong block size → TLE
Inclusive/exclusive bounds mismatch in add/del loops
Forgetting to restore `ans[idx]` after sort
Using Mo when updates exist (need Mo with updates / different technique)
`freq--` then check vs check then `--` order bugs
topics.variants:
- **Mo with updates** (time as third dimension) — heavier
- **Hilbert order** — better cache / constants
- **Rollback Mo** — only add, rollback to checkpoint (when delete hard)
- Tree Mo — §7
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: distinct values in \([l,r]\)
2. Slightly disguised: count pairs with equal values in range (freq choose 2)
3. Difficult: maintain XOR basis under add/del on range
4. Very difficult / advanced: Mo on trees / Mo with updates
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Static array; \(q=10^5\) queries ask how many values appear exactly \(k\) times in \([l,r]\).
2. Same but array updates between queries — is Mo still OK?
3. Online distinct queries stream in — Mo or persistent segtree?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: offline static ranges; add/del easy; merge hard
- Key invariant: window always equals current query range after moves
- Key formula: \(O(n\sqrt{q}\,F)\); \(B \approx n/\sqrt{q}\)
- Complexity: usually \(O(n\sqrt{n})\)
- Template to remember: sort by block, `add/del`, four while-loops

curatedProblems.insight: 3D Mo's Algorithm with point updates in O(N^(5/3)) time.

extendedTheory.overview: Square Root Decomposition partitions data of size $N$ into blocks of size $B \approx \sqrt{N}$, reducing range queries and updates to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$. Mo's Algorithm processes $Q$ offline range queries in $\mathcal{O}((N + Q)\sqrt{N})$ by ordering queries along a Hilbert space-filling curve.
keyTheorems: **Optimal Block Size:** Setting block size $B = \frac{N}{\sqrt{Q}}$ balances the total left-pointer movement ($Q \cdot B$) and right-pointer movement ($N \cdot \frac{N}{B}$), achieving minimal state transitions.

**Hilbert Curve Sorting:** Ordering queries by Hilbert curve coordinates rather than simple serpentine block indices reduces total pointer movements by $25\%–40\%$, avoiding worst-case boundary oscillations.

**Tree Mo via Euler Tour:** Flattening a tree into its DFS entry/exit tour allows arbitrary path queries $u \leftrightarrow v$ to be mapped to contiguous range queries on the tour array with an LCA parity toggle.
algorithmSteps: 1. **Query Sorting:** Sort queries $(L_i, R_i)$ primarily by $L_i / B$, and secondarily by $R_i$ (alternating ascending/descending on odd/even blocks).
2. **Two-Pointer Maintenance:** Maintain current state $[curL, curR]$ and an aggregate frequency array. Step $curL$ and $curR$ one element at a time via `add(idx)` and `remove(idx)`.
3. **Tree Path Adaptation:** If $u$ is an ancestor of $v$, query range is $[in[u], in[v]]$. Otherwise query is $[out[u], in[v]] + \{LCA(u, v)\}$. Toggle vertex presence via XOR parity.
edgeCases: In Mo's algorithm, remember to update the answer after adjusting both left and right pointers, not in between.
When removing elements, ensure counters do not decrement below 0 or access negative array indices.
For Mo's on Trees, if $u$ and $v$ have an LCA that is not $u$, the LCA node itself must be manually toggled before answering the query and toggled back immediately after.

- Prerequisites: Euler tour (entry/exit), LCA, array Mo
topics.coreIntuition: Map tree-path queries to array Mo on the **Euler tour**. One standard scheme: store entry and exit times; a path \(u\sim v\) becomes a mix of tour segments plus LCA handling. A common “tour + toggle” approach: flatten `tin`/`tout` so each node appears twice; toggling presence of a node when the Mo window crosses an occurrence puts nodes on the \(u\)–\(v\) path (with LCA carefully added/removed) into the frequency structure. Powerful but brittle — prefer HLD + segtree / binary lifting when the query is associative.

extendedTheory.overview: Square Root Decomposition partitions data of size $N$ into blocks of size $B \approx \sqrt{N}$, reducing range queries and updates to $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{N})$. Mo's Algorithm processes $Q$ offline range queries in $\mathcal{O}((N + Q)\sqrt{N})$ by ordering queries along a Hilbert space-filling curve.
keyTheorems: **Optimal Block Size:** Setting block size $B = \frac{N}{\sqrt{Q}}$ balances the total left-pointer movement ($Q \cdot B$) and right-pointer movement ($N \cdot \frac{N}{B}$), achieving minimal state transitions.

**Hilbert Curve Sorting:** Ordering queries by Hilbert curve coordinates rather than simple serpentine block indices reduces total pointer movements by $25\%–40\%$, avoiding worst-case boundary oscillations.

**Tree Mo via Euler Tour:** Flattening a tree into its DFS entry/exit tour allows arbitrary path queries $u \leftrightarrow v$ to be mapped to contiguous range queries on the tour array with an LCA parity toggle.
algorithmSteps: 1. **Query Sorting:** Sort queries $(L_i, R_i)$ primarily by $L_i / B$, and secondarily by $R_i$ (alternating ascending/descending on odd/even blocks).
2. **Two-Pointer Maintenance:** Maintain current state $[curL, curR]$ and an aggregate frequency array. Step $curL$ and $curR$ one element at a time via `add(idx)` and `remove(idx)`.
3. **Tree Path Adaptation:** If $u$ is an ancestor of $v$, query range is $[in[u], in[v]]$. Otherwise query is $[out[u], in[v]] + \{LCA(u, v)\}$. Toggle vertex presence via XOR parity.
edgeCases: In Mo's algorithm, remember to update the answer after adjusting both left and right pointers, not in between.
When removing elements, ensure counters do not decrement below 0 or access negative array indices.
For Mo's on Trees, if $u$ and $v$ have an LCA that is not $u$, the LCA node itself must be manually toggled before answering the query and toggled back immediately after.

topics.title: Sparse Table (RMQ / Idempotent Range Queries)
topics.prerequisites: Binary lifting idea, idempotent semigroup ops (min, max, gcd, AND, OR)
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: S-tier
- Frequency: Common
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1400–1900
- Prerequisites: Binary lifting idea, idempotent semigroup ops (min, max, gcd, AND, OR)
topics.coreIntuition: Precompute every interval whose length is a power of two. For idempotent ops, any \([L,R]\) is the op of **two overlapping** \(2^k\) blocks covering it — overlap is fine because \(x\oplus x=x\). That gives true \(O(1)\) queries after \(O(n\log n)\) build. No updates: if the array mutates, use a segtree/Fenwick instead.
recognitionPatterns: Static array; many range min/max/gcd queries
LCA via Euler tour + RMQ
“No updates” explicitly or array fixed after input
Need \(O(1)\) per query with comfortable \(O(n\log n)\) memory
topics.derivation:
\[
st[k][i] = \mathrm{op}(st[k-1][i], st[k-1][i+2^{k-1}])
\]
For query \([L,R]\) (0-index), \(len=R-L+1\), \(k=\lfloor\log_2 len\rfloor\):
\[
\mathrm{op}(st[k][L], st[k][R-2^k+1]).
\]
Works iff `op` is idempotent (and associative). For pure associative non-idempotent ops, use disjoint sparse table or segtree.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: \(O(n\log n)\)
- Per-query / per-operation: \(O(1)\)
- Total: \(O(n\log n + q)\)
- Memory: \(O(n\log n)\)
commonBugs: Using sparse table when updates exist
Using `+` / matrix mul with overlapping two-block query (wrong — not idempotent)
`lg` table off-by-one: must use `r-l+1`, not `r-l`
Forgetting inclusive bounds when porting from segtree habits
topics.variants:
- Index-of-minimum (store indices, compare `a[i]`)
- GCD / AND / OR sparse tables (idempotent)
- `<O(n), O(1)>` RMQ via Cartesian + LCA (overkill for CF; classic ST is enough)
- Disjoint sparse table for non-idempotent associative ops (next)
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: static range minimum queries
2. Slightly disguised: range gcd; “can all equal after range?” via min=max
3. Difficult: LCA with Euler tour + RMQ sparse table
4. Very difficult / advanced: combine with Mo / offline when static structure is one layer
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Array fixed; \(q\le 10^6\) range minimum queries — need fast answers.
2. Static array; range gcd queries.
3. Tree LCA queries with Euler tour technique.
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: static idempotent range queries
- Key invariant: two overlapping \(2^k\) blocks cover any range
- Key formula: \(k=\lfloor\log_2(r-l+1)\rfloor\)
- Complexity: build \(O(n\log n)\), query \(O(1)\)
- Template to remember: `st[k][i] = op(st[k-1][i], st[k-1][i+2^{k-1}])`

extendedTheory.overview: Advanced Data Structures encompass persistent segment trees (versioned immutability), Treaps (randomized priority binary search trees for implicit sequence operations), Cartesian Trees, and Link-Cut Trees (dynamic forest connectivity).
keyTheorems: **Path Copy Persistence:** Updating a persistent data structure creates only $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ new nodes along the modified path, sharing all unchanged subtrees with previous versions in $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ space per version.
**Treap Random Priority Balance:** Assigning uniform random priorities $\text{prio} \sim \text{Uniform}(0, 2^{31}-1)$ to each key ensures the expected tree depth is $2 \ln N \approx 1.386 \log_2 N$.
**Cartesian Tree Linear Construction:** A Cartesian tree where each node is the range minimum can be built in strictly $\mathcal{O}(N)$ time using a monotonic stack of rightmost spine ancestors.

**Link-Cut Tree Preferred Path Invariant:** Decomposing a tree into vertex-disjoint preferred paths maintained via Splay trees supports dynamic `link`, `cut`, and path aggregates in amortized $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time.
algorithmSteps: 1. **Persistent Update:** `int update(int prev, int l, int r, int pos, int val)` creates a clone node $curr$, copies children from $prev$, recursively updates the target branch, and returns $curr$.
2. **Treap Split:** `split(node, key, leftTree, rightTree)` partitions tree into keys $\le key$ and keys $> key$.
3. **Treap Merge:** `merge(node, leftTree, rightTree)` assumes all keys in $leftTree$ are smaller than $rightTree$; places highest priority at root.
extendedTheory.invariantsAndFormulas: $$\text{Depth}(\text{Treap}) = \mathcal{O}(\log N) \quad \text{(with probability } 1 - N^{-c}\text{)}, \quad \text{Space}(\text{PersistSeg}) = \mathcal{O}(N \log N + Q \log N)$$
edgeCases: Persistent segment trees over dynamic coordinate spaces require dynamic pointer allocation; allocate a pool of at least $40N$ nodes to prevent runtime memory exhaustion.
Always push lazy tags before performing `split` and `merge` in implicit Treaps (e.g. range reversals).
Link-Cut Trees require `splay(u)` and `access(u)` before querying path aggregates or modifying edges.

topics.title: Disjoint Sparse Table
topics.prerequisites: Sparse table, associative ops (semigroup), bit partitioning of ranges
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: C-tier
- Frequency: Rare
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 2000–2500
- Prerequisites: Sparse table, associative ops (semigroup), bit partitioning of ranges
topics.coreIntuition: Classic ST overlaps two blocks — fatal for non-idempotent ops like `+` or matrix multiply. A **disjoint** sparse table precomputes, for each dyadic “block boundary,” prefixes to the left and suffixes to the right so any range splits into **exactly two adjacent** precomputed halves meeting at a power-of-two aligned cut. Associativity alone suffices; idempotence not required. Still static.
recognitionPatterns: Static array; associative op; want \(O(1)\) queries without segtree
Matrix product on subarrays, non-idempotent semigroups
You already know ST and someone forbids overlapping merges
topics.derivation: Fix size \(n' = 2^{\lceil\log_2 n\rceil}\). For each level \(k\) with block length \(2^k\), at every boundary multiple of \(2^k\), store leftward suffixes and rightward prefixes under `op`. Query \([L,R]\): let \(k = \mathrm{msb}(L\oplus R)\) (highest differing bit); answer is `op(left_prefix, right_prefix)` from that level’s cut — two disjoint halves. Build \(O(n\log n)\), query \(O(1)\) op applications.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: \(O(n\log n)\) applications of `op`
- Per-query / per-operation: \(O(1)\) applications of `op`
- Total: \(O(n\log n + q)\)
- Memory: \(O(n\log n)\)
commonBugs: Using classic overlapping ST for `+` / matrix product
Empty ranges / \(l>r\) not handled
Incorrect MSB of `l^r` (`__builtin_clz` width assumptions)
Padding with wrong identity for the semigroup
topics.variants:
- Sum / product / affine composition / small matrix mul
- Fallback: iterative segtree \(O(\log n)\) query is almost always acceptable — DST is micro-opt / elegance
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: static range sum with \(O(1)\) (usually Fenwick/prefix better)
2. Slightly disguised: static range matrix product
3. Difficult: associative custom merge too fat for segtree constants (rare)
4. Very difficult / advanced: combine with monoid ideas in research-style tasks
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. Static array of \(2\times 2\) matrices; product on subarrays; \(q\) large.
2. Explain why classic sparse table fails for range sum with the two-block trick.
3. Same queries solvable by segtree — when would DST be worth coding?
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: static associative non-idempotent \(O(1)\) queries (rare)
- Key invariant: range ↔ two disjoint halves at `msb(l^r)` cut
- Key formula: `op(pref[k][l], pref[k][r])`
- Complexity: \(O(n\log n)\) build, \(O(1)\) query
- Template to remember: build inward prefixes at each dyadic mid; query via `l^r`

topics.title: Cartesian Tree
topics.prerequisites: Monotone stack, heap+BST properties, RMQ↔LCA equivalence
topics.whyItMatters:
- Contest ROI: B-tier
- Frequency: Occasional
- Typical CF/ICPC rating range: 1900–2500
- Prerequisites: Monotone stack, heap+BST properties, RMQ↔LCA equivalence
topics.coreIntuition: Build a binary tree on array indices: inorder = array order (BST on index), heap order on values (e.g. min-heap on \(a_i\)). Range minimum on \([L,R]\) is the LCA of nodes \(L\) and \(R\) in this tree. Conversely, the tree encodes nearest smaller elements: parent = nearest smaller to left/right in the stack construction. One \(O(n)\) monotone stack builds it.
recognitionPatterns: Nearest greater/smaller to left/right → tree edges
Histogram largest rectangle / contribution of each element as minimum
Want to recurse on “range split by minimum”
RMQ reductions, treap-like structure with priorities = values
topics.derivation:
Stack of indices with increasing \(a[\cdot]\) (for min-Cartesian). For each `i` left-to-right: pop until `a[stack.top()] < a[i]` (strictness = tie-break); last popped becomes left child of `i`; `i` becomes right child of new top.  
Heap property + inorder indices ⇒ for range \([L,R]\), the minimum’s index is LCA\((L,R)\). Construction \(O(n)\); then LCA via binary lifting \(O(n\log n)\) prep if needed.
topics.complexity:
- Preprocessing: \(O(n)\) build; \(+O(n\log n)\) if adding LCA
- Per-query / per-operation: \(O(1)\) / \(O(\log n)\) with LCA; or use tree DP offline
- Total: usually \(O(n)\) + tree processing
- Memory: \(O(n)\)
commonBugs: Strict vs non-strict inequality on ties (duplicate values) — define policy
Assuming root is `st.back()` instead of walking parents / `st.front()`
Confusing min-Cartesian with max-Cartesian for “nearest greater”
Using as online RMQ without LCA preprocessing
topics.variants:
- Max-Cartesian (nearest greater)
- Recursive D&C on ranges “split by minimum” without storing tree
- Bridge to treaps: random priorities ≈ Cartesian on `(key, priority)`
topics.problemPatterns:
1. Standard application: nearest smaller to left/right in one pass
2. Slightly disguised: sum of range minimums over all subarrays via contribution
3. Difficult: tree DP on Cartesian tree of the array
4. Very difficult / advanced: RMQ↔LCA reductions; persistent / offline structures on Cartesian
topics.recognitionExercises:
1. For each index, find nearest strictly smaller to the left and to the right.
2. Array; compute \(\sum_{l\le r} \min(a_l,\ldots,a_r)\) in \(O(n)\).
3. Recursively split ranges at their minimum — need the explicit tree for DP.
topics.cheatSheet:
- When to use: nearest smaller/greater, range-min D&C tree, RMQ↔LCA
- Key invariant: heap on values + inorder = indices
- Key formula: parent = nearest smaller (stack); RMQ = LCA
- Complexity: \(O(n)\) build
- Template to remember: monotone stack left-to-right linking `l`/`r`/`p`
